answer.sourceLine: Genuinely from Paul’s first letter to the church at Corinth, 1 Corinthians 13:13 (written c. 53–57 AD). This exact English wording — with “charity” rather than “love” — is the distinctive rendering of the King James Version (1611); Paul’s Greek reads πιστις, ελπις, αγαπη (faith, hope, love).

source.excerpt: And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.
trail: The verse is 1 Corinthians 13:13 — the closing line of Paul’s “love chapter.” The KJV text reads “And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (Bible Hub, KJV).

The distinctive word is “charity.” The King James translators (1611) chose it to render Greek αγαπη (agapē) here; most modern English Bibles render the same word “love” (translation comparison, Bible Study Tools).
The King James Version was first published in 1611, placing this English wording firmly in the public domain (Wikisource, KJV 1 Corinthians).
source.excerptNote: 1 Corinthians 13:13, King James Version. The 1611 first edition spelled the closing word “charitie.” Modern translations (NIV, ESV, RSV) render the same verse “And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love.”
source.rightsNote: The King James Version was first published in 1611; its text is in the public domain in the United States. (In the United Kingdom the KJV is held under perpetual Crown copyright/letters patent, but that does not affect U.S. public-domain status.) Paul’s underlying Greek is, of course, ancient and long in the public domain.

author.heading: About Paul the Apostle
author.metaLine: c. 5 – c. 64/67 AD · Apostle, missionary & author of much of the New Testament
author.bio: Paul of Tarsus was a first-century Jewish follower of Jesus whose letters to early Christian communities became foundational texts of the New Testament. His first epistle to the Corinthians contains chapter 13, the celebrated “hymn to love,” written to a divided congregation to exalt agapē above spiritual gifts. 1 Corinthians is universally counted among the seven letters scholars regard as genuinely Pauline.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Paul is correct — this really is his line. The confusion is almost entirely about the wording, because the same verse circulates in two very different English forms.

items.who: King James Version vs. modern Bibles
items.why: The famous “charity” wording is specific to the King James Version (1611). Paul’s Greek word is αγαπη (agapē), and most modern translations render the verse “the greatest of these is love” (Bible Study Tools comparison). Quoting it as “charity” is quoting the KJV specifically.
The line is frequently quoted at weddings and funerals as simply “the Bible,” but it has a precise address: 1 Corinthians 13:13, the last verse of Paul’s hymn to love (Bible Hub).

misattribution.truthLine: Correctly Paul’s — 1 Corinthians 13:13. The “charity” phrasing is the King James Version (1611); Paul’s Greek says love (Wikisource, KJV).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians to a fractious young church preoccupied with status and showy spiritual gifts. Chapter 13 — the “hymn to love” — interrupts that argument to insist that agapē outlasts prophecy, tongues, and knowledge. Verse 13 is the climax: of the three enduring things, love is supreme.

The line’s modern life is largely liturgical. It is one of the most-read passages at weddings and funerals in the English-speaking world, which is why the stately King James phrasing — “charity” — remains lodged in cultural memory even as pew Bibles now say “love.”
